findings.title: PowerShell opened LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS and read its memory on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, with a call trace ending in an UNKNOWN module (C:\windows\SYSTEM32\ntdll.dll+9c584|C:\Windows\System32\KERNELBASE.dll+2732e|UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D)), indicating injected/reflective code rather than a signed tool. Windows Security 4663 corroborates the same second: user pbeesly's powershell.exe performed 'Read from process memory' (Access Mask 0x10) on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. PowerShell 4104 script blocks from pbeesly at 03:21:29 contain a reflective loader (GetProcAddress via Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods, VirtualAlloc/CreateThread pattern) and a base64 gzip-encoded hidden powershell payload, consistent with an in-memory credential-dumping toolchain. This is LSASS memory access for credential theft.

findings.title: lsass.exe wrote the SAM account hive value on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 748, ProcessGuid {47ab858c-e6ad-5eac-0c00-000000000500}) set the registry value HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F at 2020-05-02T03:19:10.368 (Sysmon event 13, Details 'Binary Data'). This is the SAM account database value; the write occurred seconds after lsass.exe was (re)started at 03:19:09.809. No reg save / hive-copy command lines were observed (C017/C021/C023/C024 zero hits), so this is a registry-level SAM touch rather than a classic offline hive dump, but it is consistent with SAM credential material being manipulated on the host.

findings.title: lsass.exe repeatedly wrote the cached domain credential store HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 728, ProcessGuid {5aa8ec29-cad7-5eac-0c00-000000000400}) set HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 four times between 2020-05-02T03:11:40 and 03:15:03 (Sysmon event 13, Details 'Binary Data'). NL$1 is the cached domain credential (DCC2) store. The writes coincide with the window in which pbeesly was running C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua via PsExec (03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49, 03:15:03), i.e. the cached-credential registry key was being touched while the attacker's tooling was active on that host. No direct read of SECURITY\Cache was captured in the security log (C042/C043/C044 zero hits).

findings.title: Credential-access tooling staged and executed by pbeesly across scranton and nashua
findings.summary: The credential-access activity is part of a broader intrusion by user pbeesly. On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly ran Sysinternals PsExec64.exe with cleartext credentials ('-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by') to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42), and used sdelete64.exe to wipe artifacts (e.g. C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\Draft.Zip). On nashua, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe was spawned by C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe repeatedly (03:11:40-03:15:04), matching the lsass cached-credential registry writes. This establishes the actor and tooling behind the LSASS/SAM/cached-credential access.

On 2020-05-02 03:19:17 and 03:19:24 UTC, netsh.exe ran 'trace start capture=yes traceFile=...etl' and 'trace stop' on scranton.dmevals.local as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The Sysmon process-create event shows the parent process is C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service, i.e. the Azure Network Watcher extension performing a legitimate on-demand packet capture. No adversary tooling or user context is involved.
findings.title: netsh trace packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent activity

findings.summary: Between 2020-05-02 03:18:38 and 03:19:44 UTC, logman.exe created, started and stopped ETW traces (GAEvents, RTEvents, WindowsAzure-GuestAgent-Diagnostic) writing to C:\WindowsAzure\Logs on scranton.dmevals.local as SYSTEM. Every invocation's parent process is C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\WaAppAgent.exe, the Azure Windows Guest Agent, so this is platform diagnostic telemetry collection, not adversary network sniffing.
findings.title: logman trace create/start/stop on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Guest Agent diagnostics

findings.summary: The PowerShell script-block hit on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01 23:08:03 (user DMEVALS\pbeesly) is an Add-Type call whose ScriptName is C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules\PowerShellGet\1.0.0.1\PSModule.psm1, i.e. the built-in PowerShellGet module compiling a C# helper type. This is credential use/exfiltration rather than input capture, but it demonstrates credential handling by the same actor.

findings.title: No offline-cracking artifacts; lsass/SAM access is credential dumping, not cracking
findings.summary: No hashcat/Invoke-Mimikatz/DumpCreds script blocks, no ntds.dit/SAM file writes, and no secretsdump command lines were found. The lsass access on scranton.dmevals.local is a single powershell.exe (PID 3876) read with GrantedAccess 0x1000, and the SAM registry reads are performed by lsass.exe itself as SCRANTON$ (AccessMask 0xf003f) — normal OS behaviour. These are credential-dumping/access artifacts (T1003/T1552), not password cracking, and no cracking tooling or dumped-hash files appear in the data.

The 4648 explicit-credential logons (15 total) are user pbeesly authenticating with explicit credentials via PsExec (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe) on nashua.dmevals.local and from scranton.dmevals.local to target server NASHUA, plus routine winlogon/taskhostw localhost logons (DWM-1/2, UMFD-0/1/2, SCRANTON$) — lateral movement / normal logon behaviour, not MFA token or smart-card interception. No smart-card, credential-provider, or MFA-interception artifacts were observed.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe (PID 3876, running as SYSTEM) created C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk at 2020-05-02T03:04:23Z. A shortcut placed in the StartUp folder is a classic T1187 forced-authentication trigger: when the user logs on and the .lnk is resolved/opened it can cause the host to authenticate outbound (SMB/WebDAV) to an attacker-controlled target, leaking NTLM credentials. The same PowerShell session had earlier written hostui.txt into C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite\, indicating the attacker staged the hostui payload.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe ran 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' (2020-05-02T03:21:19Z), spawning C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe (PID 8452) at High integrity as DMEVALS\pbeesly. The binary masquerades as a Windows component (Company, Description, Product, OriginalFileName all '-') yet sits in System32. hostui.exe then spawned powershell.exe reading 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft' 'value Supplement' piped to Invoke-Expression, which in turn launched a hidden base64-encoded PowerShell (-nop -w hidden -e ...). This is the forced-authentication/execution chain: a fake System32 binary coerced into elevation that then executes attacker code.

findings.title: Routine svchost.exe LSASS handle opens (0x1000) are benign
findings.summary: The large majority of Sysmon event 10 hits targeting lsass.exe are svchost.exe opening LSASS with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), which is normal Windows behaviour for services querying process information. These are distinct from the full-access (0x1FFFFF) PowerShell access on scranton.

Hunting for T1539 (Steal Web Session Cookie) across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other found no access to browser cookie stores. The 13 PowerShell 4104 hits matching 'Cookies'/'Login Data' are benign Microsoft DSC module helper scripts (e.g. CommonResourceHelper.psm1, xStorage module manifests) where the word appears incidentally in module code, not cookie theft tooling. Sysmon file-create (event 11) hits for 'cookies'/'session' are OS artifacts (INetCookies package cache, UpdateSessionOrchestration.etl, SleepStudy .etl) written by svchost.exe/System, and the only browser-related process creations are normal MicrosoftEdge.exe/MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe/MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe launches by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local. No 4663 object-access events reference any browser cookie/login database, and no process command line references chrome/edge/firefox cookie paths. The genuine malicious activity on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly) is APT29-style PowerShell — screen capture, keystroke/AV check, and 7-Zip exfil to a WebDAV share — which is credential/collection activity but not web session cookie theft.
